title: Compound Growth
summary: START NOW → LET TIME WORK → WATCH FEES → STAY THE COURSE
subtitle: Fourteen modules back, this course started with a pay stub. Every module since had one idea sitting quietly underneath it.

blocks.text: Fourteen lessons back, this course started with a pay stub.
Since then, you’ve met the TFSA, RRSP, FHSA, RESP, RDSP and RRIF. You’ve learned about fees, ETFs and risk. Every one of those lessons had one idea sitting quietly underneath it, never fully named.

That idea is compound growth. It’s why starting early matters more than almost anything else in this course. It’s why a fee gap of a percent or two can turn into six figures. It’s why tax-sheltered accounts exist at all. This lesson names it and shows why it has been the engine behind everything else you’ve learned.
Put time on your side, and your money starts doing more of the work.
blocks.detail: Once you see how growth builds on growth, starting early and keeping fees low stop being rules and start being obvious.
blocks.extra: Section 03 shows it happening, year by year.

blocks.text: Simple growth is straightforward: you earn a return on what you put in, every year, on the same original amount.

Compound growth is different. You earn a return on your original amount plus a return on all the growth so far. Every year, the base you earn on gets a little bigger, not because you added money, but because last year’s growth is now part of this year’s base.
That’s the whole idea. It sounds small. Over enough years, it isn’t.

items.title: “Compound growth mostly just means my money grows steadily over time.”
items.text: Steady growth and compound growth are different shapes. Steady growth is a straight line. Compound growth curves upward, slowly at first, then steeply, because the base it’s worked out on keeps getting bigger. Most of the growth in a long-term investment happens in the later years, not the early ones.

blocks.text: Picture $10,000 invested, earning 7% a year and left untouched.
$10,000 at 7% a year, nothing added
blocks.detail: Balance, and growth in that single year

blocks.text: Look at the growth in a single year. By year thirty, it’s nearly four times what it was in year ten, on the same original $10,000, with nothing added. That’s not a higher return. It’s the same 7%, working on a base that quietly grew huge in the background.
CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: THE RULE OF 72

Here’s a shortcut to carry with you: divide 72 by your yearly return, and the answer is roughly how many years it takes your money to double. At 7%, that’s 72 ÷ 7, just over ten years, which matches the table: $10,000 grew to $19,672 by year ten, a hair under double. Try it on a fee. A 2% fee that cuts a 7% return to 5% doesn’t just cost 2% a year. It stretches the doubling time from about ten years to about fourteen and a half. No calculator needed, just one number that turns the Investment Fees lesson into something you can work out on a napkin.

sections.title: Why the first ten years matter more than they look like they do

blocks.text: CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: WHY THE FIRST TEN YEARS MATTER MORE THAN THEY LOOK LIKE THEY DO

Here’s what catches people off guard: in the example above, the account looks unimpressive for a long time. It takes ten full years to grow by less than $10,000, which can feel slow. But those quiet early years aren’t wasted. They build the base that later growth compounds on. Skip them, by starting ten years later, and you don’t just lose ten years of deposits. You lose ten years of compounding on those deposits, which is a much bigger loss than it looks. That’s why so many lessons in this course said to open the account now, even with a small first deposit. The TFSA, FHSA, RESP and RDSP lessons all said a version of it. Now you know why: the quiet early years do more work than they seem to.
You can’t control the market’s return. But two things you do control matter a great deal to how compound growth plays out.

Time. The longer money stays invested, the more years compounding has to work. That’s why time horizon, from the Risk Tolerance lesson, is such a central question. It isn’t only about risk. It’s about how much room compounding has.

Fees. The Investment Fees lesson showed a fee gap of under 2% growing into a gap of nearly $290,000 over 25 years. That’s the same idea as this lesson, working in reverse. A fee doesn’t just cost the fee. It costs every year of compounding that money would have earned.

Tax is a third lever. In a regular, taxable account, part of each year’s growth goes to tax, so less is left to compound. Inside a TFSA, RRSP or FHSA, the full amount keeps growing. That’s the real reason those accounts are worth opening early: they let compounding work on every dollar.

items.title: “A slightly higher fee is a minor tradeoff if the fund performs a little better.”
items.text: Because fees compound in reverse, a small fee difference can outweigh years of slightly better results. The fee is certain and permanent. The extra performance is neither. It’s the same math as the Investment Fees lesson, seen from the growth side.

items.title: I understand growth compounds on growth, not just on my original contributions.
I know early years often look unimpressive, and that this is normal, not a sign something is wrong.
I’ve opened the accounts I qualify for, even with small first deposits, instead of waiting until I feel ready.
I understand why the fee comparison in the Investment Fees lesson matters so much. Fees compound too, just in the wrong direction.
I’m thinking about my investments in terms of years, not months.

blocks.text: The twins, ten years apart
paragraphs: Elin and Karin were twin sisters who grew up in Thunder Bay. At twenty-two, Elin landed her first job at a credit union and set up an automatic $200 a month into her TFSA. Karin, working retail and saving for a trip to Iceland, said she would start once life settled down.
Every few years, Elin nudged her. Karin always had a reason to wait: the trip, then a car, then a move to Winnipeg. At thirty-two, newly promoted, she finally sat down to start.

That night she almost talked herself out of it again. Elin was ten years ahead. What was the point of starting now? Then Elin showed her the math on a napkin, and Karin made her choice. She set up the same $200 a month, and promised herself she would never stop it for twenty-five years.
Elin had her own decision to make. At forty-seven, after twenty-five years of saving, she had about $162,000, assuming 7% a year. She decided to stop adding money and leave the account alone.

Here was the twist. At fifty-seven, Karin finished her own twenty-five years with the same $200 a month and the same 7%, and her account held the same $162,000. But Elin’s, left untouched for ten more years, had grown to about $325,000. Same deposits, same years of saving. Elin’s money had a ten-year head start.
Karin wasn’t bitter. She framed the napkin and gave it to her niece on her eighteenth birthday, with a note that said: “Start at twenty-two. Ask your mother why.”

blocks.text: Compound growth means earning returns on your returns, not just on your deposits. That’s why growth speeds up in later years, after quietly building a base in the early ones. Time and fees are the two levers you control: more time means more years of compounding, and lower fees mean less of it lost along the way. Starting now, even with a small amount, beats waiting for a better moment almost every time.
Start now, even small, and give your money the head start it needs.
blocks.detail: Every year you begin earlier gives compounding another year to work on everything you’ve saved.
blocks.extra: Section 08 helps you map your own compounding timeline.

items.title: Compound growth
items.text: Growth worked out on your deposits plus all the growth so far, not on the original amount alone.

items.title: Base
items.text: The total that growth is worked out on in a given year. It rises as past growth adds up.

items.title: Time horizon
items.text: How long until you need the money, and so how many years compounding has to work.
